name: The Chalk Line Edicts — Shelf Floor Text Movement
creator: Anonymous; attributed to a loosely organized network called 'The Scribes'
description: Beginning in 2196, anonymous Shelf residents began writing dense, legally precise text in chalk and thermite-pen on public floors, staircases, and transit platforms — formatted as corporate contracts, eviction notices, and corponation charters, but with the actual terms of Shelf life written in without euphemism. A staircase in the Ochota-Shelf district famously displayed a full 40-meter 'lease agreement' in which the tenant agrees to 'accept structural collapse, water contamination, and respiratory illness as standard features of the unit.' The movement spread to 14 Shelf sectors within two years.
cultural_impact: The Chalk Line Edicts became a template for Shelf legal literacy campaigns; several community advocates began distributing actual contract-reading workshops in the wake of the movement's visibility.
controversy: Meridian 88 Civic Authority classified thermite-pen text as 'permanent structural vandalism' and began prosecuting Scribes under corporate property statutes; three known participants received neural-restriction sentences.
story_hooks: A Civic Authority investigator tasked with identifying the Scribes finds herself reading the floor texts on her commute and begins leaving corrections to the corporate language — then realizes someone is correcting her corrections.
A Scribe is caught and offered immunity in exchange for naming collaborators; the network must decide whether to trust that she won't talk or preemptively disavow her.
A Tier 4 property developer buys a Shelf building specifically because a famous Chalk Line Edict text is on its staircase floor, intending to sell it as luxury heritage — and the Scribes respond.
